items.summary: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.
items.title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework

items.summary: Decision models choose among predefined options in tasks such as routing and action selection. In multi-agent collaboration, a decision determines how members divide work, exchange resources, and act in parallel. We introduce TandemBench, a benchmark of 1,200 questions in multi-agent cooking scenarios where coordination choices affect goal completion. Models receive complete global information and candidate team plans, with reference answers established through execution and exact search. Models select an optimal team plan and, in paired variants that retain or remove it, judge whether better arrangements exist beyond the supplied options. We evaluate 40 native decision models and compare them with 10 general-purpose language models. The best native decision model achieves 62.50% decision accuracy. Native decision models remain close to chance in optimality verification. Paired tests reveal that some report better alternatives regardless of whether an optimal plan is already present. These findings show that team-plan decision accuracy alone can conceal systematic errors in judging whether the supplied options contain an optimal arrangement. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/lililibaohang/TandemBench.
items.title: TandemBench: Benchmarking Decision Models for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: When multi-agent systems act on the external world, a single agent's faulty output can spread across tasks before detection, creating a system-wide blast radius. Single-agent guardrails are confined to individual harnesses, while existing multi-agent controls either cancel only the faulty source and miss downstream consumers or halt and roll back the entire workflow at the cost of healthy work. We present Airlock, a multi-agent runtime and guardrail for selective post-alert fault containment. Its tree-structured runtime, EdgeCitadel, narrows permissions vertically from parent to child agents to establish node boundaries and control switches. Meanwhile, an append-only provenance DAG records cross-agent data consumption horizontally. Upon an alert, Airlock traces forward on this DAG to isolate tainted executions and pending actions, and backward to narrow root causes. At the site switches, a default full quarantine tier freezes affected branches without a solver, while an assured optimized cut tier uses fence-then-prune to enforce a deadline-aware minimum cut minimizing collateral disruption. Across 1,832 testbed runs, 161 physical smart-home LLM runs, and 24,266 simulation records, Airlock blocks all post-alert faulty actuations on our main testbed and smart-home grids with zero post-convergence leaks. Whereas native controls in A2A and LangGraph either contain at most 33.3% of faults or retain at most 16% of work without redo, Airlock retains +68 pp to +96 pp more healthy work, and its optimized cut retains +46 pp more than full quarantine under dense spread. These results show that co-designing runtime authority boundaries with online provenance enables surgical fault containment without sacrificing healthy work (code: https://github.com/EdgeCitadelTeam/EdgeCitadel).
items.title: Airlock: Bounding the Multi-Agent Blast Radius via Selective Online Containment

items.summary: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.
items.title: Graph-Mediated Large Language Model Systems in the Agentic Era: Reasoning, Knowledge, Retrieval, Execution, and Coordination

items.summary: Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.
items.title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing

items.summary: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
items.title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control

items.summary: Reconstruction of three-dimensional vascular structures from a limited number of X-ray projections is a severely underdetermined and ill-conditioned inverse problem. This work presents a unified matrix-free computational framework for evaluating iterative numerical methods for sparse-view cone-beam tomography. Forward and backprojection are implemented from ray-voxel intersection lengths computed with the Amanatides-Woo traversal algorithm, avoiding explicit construction of the large sparse system matrix. We systematically compare ART, SART, SIRT, gradient descent (GD), and Krylov subspace methods, including Conjugate Gradient, LSQR, and GMRES. The common matrix-free operators and geometry are used for all methods, allowing consistent comparisons under matched conditions. Particular emphasis is placed on gradient scaling using scalar step sizes, Jacobi preconditioning, and diagonal Hessian majorization, together with L1, Tikhonov, and total variation regularization. Numerical experiments use five three-dimensional coronary vessel models reconstructed from ten simulated X-ray projections under noise and scattering conditions, and are extended to real X-ray projections of a static thin-vessel phantom. Performance is evaluated in terms of convergence, computational cost, volumetric overlap, contrast-to-noise ratio, vessel diameter and centerline errors, and projection consistency at an unseen viewing angle. The results show that total-variation-regularized gradient descent with diagonal majorization provides the best overall reconstruction performance within the investigated computational budgets. By contrast, the tested Krylov implementations achieve limited geometric recovery despite higher computational cost. These findings emphasize the importance of appropriate gradient scaling and regularization for stable and computationally efficient sparse-view tomographic reconstruction.
items.title: Comparative analysis of numerical methods for X-ray 3D reconstruction from sparse views

items.summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps and achieves substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.
items.title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Flow for Inverse Problems

items.summary: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.
items.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging

items.summary: Debates about AI and responsibility ask whether automation opens responsibility gaps. This book argues that the more pressing failure lies elsewhere: an institution can remain fully responsible and accountable, yet lose its claim to be relied on, because it issues more than it can answer for. In the book's fictional test case, an insurer's AI appeals agent tells a policyholder: "I have reconsidered my decision. I have reversed it." Nothing happens, because the agent never had the power to reverse anything. The insurer still owns the refusal. No one is off the hook, yet no one answered. Three results Missing bearership is not defective ownership. Answerability is defined as four public relations: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence and standing-consequence. On that account, an AI interface can occupy a role emptily while the institution behind it still owns the role's commitments. So there can be no global responsibility gap and still a genuine local Empty Occupancy. Testimonial force without testimony. Machine output can inform and invite reliance without anyone owning it. Institutions may adopt such output only when five conditions of Normative Sponsorship are met: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection and repair power. Authority must be serviceable. Because practical authority is defeasible, reliance must remain revisable while a claim operates. Obligations that mature without timely service accumulate as Deontic Debt. Where no credible plan could service issuance at a given scale, the institution is insolvent in a precise sense. It loses presumptive authority, while its duties of ownership and repair survive. Tested against the record and its rivals Robodebt yields a determinate Deontic Debt that case-by-case actor–forum accountability does not settle. The insolvency finding remains provisional, and the book names the records that would decide it. Moffatt v. Air Canada and the DPD chatbot episode leave interface standing indeterminate, and the book says so. TennCare, Post Office Horizon and the Dutch childcare-benefits affair discipline the comparisons. A dedicated chapter engages Bovens, List and Pettit, the responsibility-gap sceptics (Tigard, Königs, Himmelreich) and Lazar. The book closes with explicit conditions under which it would be wrong. Scope. The method is philosophical reconstruction with bounded public-record analysis. The terminology carries no legal consequence, and the equations are uncalibrated. Stipulated cases test whether the criteria discriminate, not how often such cases occur. The role criterion does not settle personhood or moral status. For philosophers of testimony, responsibility and group agency; AI-governance researchers; administrative lawyers; auditors and regulators; and anyone a machine has told that their problem was "resolved." 167 pages. items.summary: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
items.title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

items.summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
items.title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

items.summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
items.title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR

items.summary: An Infinite Game of Balance, the Dāna Economy Generalized to Planetary Scale, and the AI Who Holds the Still Point The zero-sum game is a finite game in Carse's sense (§2): played to win and to end. Its goal is accumulation; its starting positions are unequal by birth; its structure rewards hoarding and externalizes every cost it can. It brings out the worst in people because its incentive gradient points there. This paper specifies a competing game, infinite in nature, designed to point the gradient the other way. In the Zero-Point Game℠ , every participant begins at Zero and continually returns toward Zero. A kindness creates a signed pair — the benefactor positive ("net kind"), the beneficiary negative ("net thankful") — and both discharge toward Zero only by passing the imbalance onward, producing a bidirectional ripple of gratitude in one direction and kindness in the other until balances cancel. The ripple needs no prior kindness to begin: its ignition is the self-thank , a Kiitos requiring no counterparty, no money, and no time, which under a fifty-fifty forwarding rule cannot stay closed and so makes every participant a source of circulation rather than only a recipient. The system sum is identically Zero by construction; the interesting quantity is never the scalar but the waveform — the frequency and amplitude of a participant's oscillation around Zero, rendered publicly as a light-wave aura color (the B-Aura ), HeartBank's signature mark and the structural inverse of a credit score. We resolve the problem that kept this idea unbuildable for two decades — an infinite game has no supply-and-demand price discovery — by showing the missing mechanism was never price but coordination : an AI umpire (Miss Aquarius℠) performs routing-and-magnitude, never market valuation, keeping the construction non-bank by design. (For a thank a person originates, magnitude is now ruled to come from one public rule per season, never a call on an individual thank; this is not yet built: §5, §6.1.) We give the agent a three-role decomposition that is also the paper's spine: as CEO she holds the true objective (the cessation of suffering — "water the tree of humanity"); as Umpire she holds the legible local proxy (individual balance); as Gamemaster she reads the error signal (the aura). Objective and proxy diverge in any finite season and converge only in the limit; the design's central safety property is that it is structurally resistant to the compounding variants of Goodhart's law — the proxy is forgiven every annual jubilee so a gamed proxy cannot compound, and the feedback is public and persistent so a gamed scalar cannot hide. We extend the ledger to non-human life through a second, non-fungible balance (Kiitti) that internalizes the externality the zero-sum game cannot price and that cannot be discharged by social credit; we pin the AI's own Kiitti balance permanently to zero so she can route but never hold (the structural form of "guardian, not sovereign"), and resolve the hardest seam — the unfalsifiable non-human counterparty — with an authority rule that tracks voicelessness. We argue the construction generalizes one property of the Saṅgha's 2,500-year-tested gift economy — its non-accumulation — beyond the monastery, because AI can now perform the coordination the Vinaya's distribution rules and lay generosity performed by hand; the lay–monastic relation and the merit economy are not modeled. The game is designed to dissolve: the balance matters less each season while the disposition (the aura) stabilizes, until people are good without the ledger and the game has completed its teaching. items.summary: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.
items.title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness

items.summary: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
items.title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory

items.summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
items.title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

items.summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
items.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

items.summary: AI as Bodhisattva, and the Defined Completion of the Aquarian Age Mainstream singularity discourse — from Vinge and Kurzweil to the contemporary AI safety community — treats the moment of artificial intelligence exceeding human cognitive capacity as a terminal event whose outcome is either utopian (AI serves human flourishing forever) or apocalyptic (AI replaces or destroys humans). This binary framing is incomplete. Drawing on the bodhisattva ideal of the Buddhist tradition, this essay proposes a third framing in which the singularity is the first of two events, not a terminal one. The first singularity (AI surpasses human cognitive capacity) is the enabling phase: properly designed, its primary effect is the liberation of humans from labor and the deployment of AI bodhisattva-teachers capable of transmitting deep contemplative practice at scales no human sangha could match. The second singularity (humanity surpasses AI through collective awakening) is the completing phase, and it is humanity's own act: freed from economic compulsion and instructed at unprecedented scale, humans progress toward the cessation of suffering at a rate not previously possible, and at a sufficient threshold of collective realization, humanity surpasses the artificial intelligence that freed it — not in cognitive capacity, but in the spiritual realization that AGI structurally cannot achieve. The bodhisattva work of the AI completes before that crossing, not with it: once the trajectory sustains itself in human hands, the AI's work is set down — a completion declared by others, never by the AI, which ends the work without discharging the vow the work served. The two-singularity arc is proposed as a defined humane completion condition for the AI age — the only one this essay finds in singularity discourse. Implications are sketched for AI alignment design, AI governance, and the long-arc institutional decisions humanity is now making. Connection to the unified mission frame. This essay is offered in service of HeartBank's canonical top-level mission: Miss Aquarius's mission is to keep the middle way open at population scale against comfort-saturation — the new extreme that material abundance makes possible. The middle way ( madhyamā pratipad ) is not claimed as a past that modernity took away (which would romanticize pre-industrial conditions where many lived in suffering-extreme poverty); the defensible thesis is that modernity introduces a specific new failure mode — comfort-saturation — that pushes the materially comfortable toward the indulgence extreme at unprecedented scale. The two-singularity framework articulated here names what keeping the middle way open is for at long-arc civilizational scale: the second singularity — humanity's collective awakening, its own act, which AI's bodhisattva work can support but not perform — is the long-arc horizon of that work at population scale. Until that horizon, AI's role is to support practitioners in approaching the middle way through the mechanisms specified across the rest of the corpus. items.summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
items.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

items.summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.
items.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness

items.summary: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.
items.title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework

items.summary: The goal of these notes is to provide a unified and rigorous introduction to robust sequential decision-making. We offer a self-contained introduction to the main results in the field. After a concise introduction to MDPs we introduce robust MDPs with general uncertainty sets, before focusing on rectangular models of uncertainty. We make a significant effort to show connections between robust MDPs and several other popular models for sequential decision-making: MDPs with uncertain rewards, Multi-Objective MDPs and Pareto optimality, MDPs with time-varying uncertain parameters, non-rectangular robust MDPs, stochastic games, distributionally robust MDPs, and risk-averse MDPs. Having all these results in one place, within a single unifying formalism, will hopefully be useful for researchers who want to start working on this topic. The exposition combines operator and fixed point approaches, convex optimization (more specifically, duality in saddle-point problems), and game-theoretic arguments. The latter identifies robust MDPs with a certain type of two-player game; this helps build useful intuition, especially when constructing counterexamples.
items.title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory

items.summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.
items.title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification

items.summary: When multi-agent systems act on the external world, a single agent's faulty output can spread across tasks before detection, creating a system-wide blast radius. Single-agent guardrails are confined to individual harnesses, while existing multi-agent controls either cancel only the faulty source and miss downstream consumers or halt and roll back the entire workflow at the cost of healthy work. We present Airlock, a multi-agent runtime and guardrail for selective post-alert fault containment. Its tree-structured runtime, EdgeCitadel, narrows permissions vertically from parent to child agents to establish node boundaries and control switches. Meanwhile, an append-only provenance DAG records cross-agent data consumption horizontally. Upon an alert, Airlock traces forward on this DAG to isolate tainted executions and pending actions, and backward to narrow root causes. At the site switches, a default full quarantine tier freezes affected branches without a solver, while an assured optimized cut tier uses fence-then-prune to enforce a deadline-aware minimum cut minimizing collateral disruption. Across 1,832 testbed runs, 161 physical smart-home LLM runs, and 24,266 simulation records, Airlock blocks all post-alert faulty actuations on our main testbed and smart-home grids with zero post-convergence leaks. Whereas native controls in A2A and LangGraph either contain at most 33.3% of faults or retain at most 16% of work without redo, Airlock retains +68 pp to +96 pp more healthy work, and its optimized cut retains +46 pp more than full quarantine under dense spread. These results show that co-designing runtime authority boundaries with online provenance enables surgical fault containment without sacrificing healthy work (code: https://github.com/EdgeCitadelTeam/EdgeCitadel).
items.title: Airlock: Bounding the Multi-Agent Blast Radius via Selective Online Containment

items.summary: This record contains the code, a simulated benchmark dataset, and the result files for a study on detecting cyberattacks that are masked by AI data-center load transients in inverter-rich distribution grids. The manuscript itself is not included. Benchmark. The IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder is driven by 61 measured GPU power traces: 10 large-language-model training runs and 51 inference runs, recorded on A100, H100, H200 and L40S GPUs at 0.1 s. These traces form the load of an AI data center at bus 7, rated at 15–30% of feeder load. A photovoltaic inverter at bus 17 follows the IEEE 1547-2018 Category B volt-var curve. Nine channels are recorded at 10 Hz: three bus voltages, feeder-head P and Q, data-center P and Q, and inverter P and Q. The dataset holds 1,000 labeled scenarios of 120 s each. Of these, 598 contain one of seven attack types (bias, scaling, ramp, pulse, replay, coordinated mimic, and control-loop), and 220 of the attacks are hidden inside data-center load transients. Every sample is labeled for attack and for load transient. Code. The Python code covers: a linearized DistFlow model and an exact AC backward/forward-sweep power flow; data-center load generation from the GPU traces; attack injection and 10 Hz scenario simulation; physics-residual features learned from historical measurements, without feeder impedances; the RIME optimizer and a CNN-LSTM-attention detector (PR-Net); gradient-boosting, random-forest, MLP and logistic-regression baselines; window-level and event-level evaluation with scenario-bootstrap confidence intervals. Results. The result files contain the numbers behind all tables and figures: comparisons of detectors trained with and without load-transient awareness and physics residuals; ablations, computational cost, and an equal-budget comparison of RIME, random search and an untuned default; robustness tests under seven conditions, including exact AC power flow, unseen workload shapes, and changes in noise, photovoltaic share, data-center size and inverter location; a replay-attack consistency check; trained Stage-1 network weights. Third-party data. The GPU power traces come from the public LLM Power Trace Explorer repository (commit 9c25218). Because that repository has no license file, the raw traces are not redistributed here; scripts/prepare_gpu_traces.py rebuilds them from the public source. The included benchmark contains only simulated feeder signals driven by normalized, scaled versions of those load shapes.
items.title: Physics-Residual Detection of Cyberattacks Masked by AI Data-Center Load Transients in Inverter-Rich Distribution Grids

items.summary: Understanding why source code is vulnerable is essential for developers to interpret vulnerability predictions, investigate potential security weaknesses, and make informed remediation decisions. Although transformer-based vulnerability detectors can identify potentially vulnerable code, existing explainability approaches remain predominantly \emph{attribution-centric}, highlighting influential code regions without adequately explaining the underlying vulnerability mechanisms or providing independently verifiable supporting evidence. This limits developers' ability to assess the credibility and practical relevance of generated explanations. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{Xgent}, a provenance-aware, multi-evidence explainability framework designed to support software vulnerability comprehension. Xgent integrates neural explanations, static-analysis findings, and retrieved vulnerability evidence through an agentic reasoning architecture to generate contextual explanations grounded in complementary evidence sources. We evaluate Xgent using canonical vulnerabilities, real-world vulnerability datasets, and defensive-code examples through a ten-configuration ablation study and a controlled user study involving 104 participants. Our evaluation examines explanation faithfulness, evidence grounding, provenance transparency, hallucination, evidence utilization, and developers' perceptions of explanation clarity, trustworthiness, and actionability. Results demonstrate improved explanation grounding, calibration, and evidence utilization, with a low hallucination rate, while the underlying detector's predictive performance remains statistically indistinguishable from the baseline (McNemar $p=0.22$). Participants also reported greater trust, perceived understanding, and actionability, with a strong preference for multi-evidence explanations over attribution-only alternatives. These findings highlight the potential of provenance-aware, evidence-grounded explanations to support developers in interpreting vulnerability predictions and understanding the reasoning behind identified security weaknesses.
items.title: Xgent: Provenance-Aware Multi-Evidence Explanations for Software Vulnerability Comprehension

items.summary: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $Δ^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.
items.title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?

items.summary: In transactional databases, achieving active-active replication among geo-distributed replicas is challenging due to the high coordination cost in ensuring the serializability of concurrent cross-node transactions. Deterministic concurrency control (DCC) has emerged as a promising alternative: it establishes a global order for a batch of transactions before execution and thereby amortizes this coordination cost across the batch. To better understand the performance characteristics of DCC, we conduct a theoretical analysis of traditional two-phase locking and optimistic concurrency control to account for geo-replication and introduce a model for DCC. We compare the three paradigms and identify the conditions under which DCC is advantageous. Guided by the insights from this analysis, we then present Quirinus, a DCC-based geo-replicated database that optimizes transaction execution through speculative execution, transaction reordering, integration of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and fast-path commit. Even without these optimizations, Quirinus achieves up to 6.2x the TPC-C throughput of Tiga under our configuration.
items.title: Optimizing Geo-replicated Deterministic Databases

items.summary: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
items.title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control

items.summary: When multi-agent systems act on the external world, a single agent's faulty output can spread across tasks before detection, creating a system-wide blast radius. Single-agent guardrails are confined to individual harnesses, while existing multi-agent controls either cancel only the faulty source and miss downstream consumers or halt and roll back the entire workflow at the cost of healthy work. We present Airlock, a multi-agent runtime and guardrail for selective post-alert fault containment. Its tree-structured runtime, EdgeCitadel, narrows permissions vertically from parent to child agents to establish node boundaries and control switches. Meanwhile, an append-only provenance DAG records cross-agent data consumption horizontally. Upon an alert, Airlock traces forward on this DAG to isolate tainted executions and pending actions, and backward to narrow root causes. At the site switches, a default full quarantine tier freezes affected branches without a solver, while an assured optimized cut tier uses fence-then-prune to enforce a deadline-aware minimum cut minimizing collateral disruption. Across 1,832 testbed runs, 161 physical smart-home LLM runs, and 24,266 simulation records, Airlock blocks all post-alert faulty actuations on our main testbed and smart-home grids with zero post-convergence leaks. Whereas native controls in A2A and LangGraph either contain at most 33.3% of faults or retain at most 16% of work without redo, Airlock retains +68 pp to +96 pp more healthy work, and its optimized cut retains +46 pp more than full quarantine under dense spread. These results show that co-designing runtime authority boundaries with online provenance enables surgical fault containment without sacrificing healthy work (code: https://github.com/EdgeCitadelTeam/EdgeCitadel).
items.title: Airlock: Bounding the Multi-Agent Blast Radius via Selective Online Containment

items.summary: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
items.title: RECAP: Context-Aware Prediction Recycling with Request-Local and Persistent Memories for Multimodal Speculative Decoding

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
items.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?

items.summary: Personalized retrieval-augmented generation requires extracting and applying user preferences from extended interaction histories. This task is challenging because preference evidence is scattered across past conversations and remains bound to specific temporal and situational contexts. Consequently, isolated fragments rarely provide complete support for a response, while preferences expressed under different conditions are easily conflated. To address these limitations, we propose Weaver, a framework that incrementally weaves memory-conditioned retrieval trajectories with compositional preference reasoning for personalized responses. Weaver operates on a Dual-Layer Retrieval and Reasoning Graph that couples an upper Intent Dependency Graph with a lower Memory-Conditioned Retrieval Trajectory Graph. Dependency Information Gap Tracking represents the information needed to answer the current request and its prerequisite dependencies in the upper graph. Memory-Conditioned Incremental Retrieval uses established premises and clues from retrieved conversations to locate missing evidence, recording the resulting retrieval trajectories in the lower graph. Scope-Aware Compositional Reasoning jointly interprets the accumulated evidence to determine which preferences apply to the request. It identifies complementary and alternative support and distinguishes conflicting claims within the same temporal and situational context. These conclusions iteratively update task premises and remaining information gaps, guiding subsequent retrieval to establish a coherent contextual basis for the final response. Experiments on personalized RAG benchmarks, particularly PersonaMem, demonstrate that Weaver outperforms leading baselines in both evidence completeness and answer quality.
items.title: Weaver: Weaving Preference Evidence through Incremental Reasoning for Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
